item.title: I went hands-on with the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones, and they bring two very cool display features I wish were on every Android phone
item.dc:content:
It's not much of a surprise, but Xiaomi's latest flagship is the first smartphone to hit the market featuring the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have just dropped in China, but I got a quick hands-on with the devices at Snapdragon Summit after Qualcomm flew me out to check out the latest chips, devices, and innovations.

There's a lot to like about these phones, from the powerful new chipsets to the rear display surrounding the cameras. But one of its most compelling features isn't quite as obvious, and it both borrows from and improves on one of our favorite new Samsung features.

On the surface, the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones don't look much different from their predecessors. The design is nearly identical to the Xiaomi 17 Pro series, from the thick, boxy design to the rear camera display. However, this also gives users outside China a chance to experience this unique smartphone feature, since last year's model was exclusive to China.

In hand, the Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max are rather thick, but they're surprisingly light despite this. It's not much of a surprise, given the massive 7,000mAh and 8,500mAh silicon-carbon batteries in the 18 Pro and Pro Max, respectively. This is up to 1,000mAh more than the 17 Pro series.

Most of the colors are pretty standard, although the Galaxy Blue option has a rather unique design that's honestly quite striking, especially in sunlight. There's also a transparent option that gives both Nothing and Product(Red) vibes, and it's probably the one I would buy.

The rear 2.7-inch display is interesting because it adds a bit more personality to the phone, with a selection of wallpapers to choose from. It also allows users to check notifications, toggle various features, and even take selfies. That last part is particularly compelling, as it lets you take advantage of the rear 200MP cameras to preview and capture high-quality selfies.

Xiaomi also says you'll be able to utilize AI features using the rear display. I imagine adding these functions onto a smaller 120Hz panel can help with battery preservation, not that the Xiaomi 18 Pro needs it.

In many ways, it reminds me of the cover screen on flip phones like the Motorola Razr Ultra 2026. I mostly use my Razr while closed, utilizing the cover screen to open apps, respond to messages, and take selfies. However, for anyone not interested in foldables, the Xiaomi 18 Pro feels like a viable alternative, especially since you don't have to deal with the compromises that come with having a flip phone (fewer cameras, less internal space for batteries, etc.).

But the rear display is hardly the coolest or most useful feature on the Xiaomi 18 Pro series. Following Samsung's lead from the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Xiaomi equipped these phones with its own Privacy Display, which it claims is more effective than Samsung's. This is due to the unique pixel arrangement of the display, allowing Xiaomi to utilize the feature without compromising on the display quality.

It's also very customizable, going beyond just hiding apps or notifications and allowing users to hide split-screen apps or even floating apps. It's quite compelling, and I'm glad to see this feature come to more Android smartphones.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is available now in China, with a global launch happening later this year. Xiaomi hasn't told me when the phones will come to global markets, but it's very likely that North America won't be part of the global expansion plans. Still, with the latest AI chip from Qualcomm, powerful Leica cameras, and two compelling displays, the Xiaomi 18 Pro series is definitely one to look out for when the global launch comes around.
item.description: The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is the first to feature Qualcomm's latest flagship Snapdragon chips, and both phones feature two very compelling displays on the front and back.
item.author: derrek.lee@futurenet.com (Derrek Lee)
item.dc:creator: Derrek Lee
item.dc:description: <p>Derrek has had a long-time interest in mobile technology since the age of 12, which came out of his love for Nokia phones, particularly models like the Nokia N90. Since then, he closely followed the evolution of tech and the transition of Nokia from Symbian to Windows Phone, which eventually led him to Android with phones like the Moto X Pure Edition and LG G5. Since 2013, Derrek has dipped in and out of tech journalism as nothing more than a passion project while receiving his Bachelor of Arts degree in Film &amp; Digital Media at the University of California, Santa Cruz. That is until 2020, when he became the news editor for Android Central, guiding the team's coverage of Google, Android, Wear OS, and related topics. Now, as managing editor, Derrek guides the site's editorial content and direction, helping the team reach and resonate with readers, old and new, who are just as passionate about tech as we are.</p> <p>Throughout his time at Android Central, he has reviewed many products, from phones to smartwatches, smart scales, and even smart rings, establishing himself as an expert with these devices. As a fitness enthusiast, Derrek always looks for ways to incorporate tech into his life by closely examining the intersection of fitness and tech. He is also very passionate about tech being financially accessible, which often drives his decision-making in the types of products he tests out and what he recommends.</p>

item.title: 'We heard you, we heard media, we heard analysts': Motorola talks about why now is the time North America needs its premium Signature 27 phone
item.dc:content:
Earlier this week at Qualcomm's annual Snapdragon Summit, Motorola surprised many people by announcing that the flagship Signature 27 is coming to North America. This is a big deal because the last-gen Motorola Signature didn't make its way stateside, despite being pretty well received for its premium design and excellent cameras.

Interestingly, this is also the first time I've seen Motorola at Snapdragon Summit as a featured OEM, which suggests Motorola is really excited about the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and its capabilities.

I sat down with Nicole Hagen, the executive director and head of Global Product Marketing at Motorola, to talk about why now is the right time for Motorola's return to traditional smartphone flagships and what we can expect from the Signature 27.

Motorola has heard us

Motorola has always taken a regional approach to its device launches. Many devices that come to Europe or Latin America aren't available in North America, and vice versa. As a result, we miss out on plenty of models, including flagships like the original Motorola Signature, which disappointed me and many others. However, Motorola seems to have gotten the message loud and clear.

"We heard you, we heard media, we heard analysts, and I'll be honest, we even heard from a lot of customers in North America on kind of popular feedback forums that they were disappointed," Hagen told me.

"We felt that this year we have the right product with the right specs, with the right capabilities and experiences, and we think that this product is really going to resonate well amongst users looking for a premium flagship phone and perhaps something a little bit different than what they've been offered over the last few years."

She tells me Motorola even saw Signature devices registered in the U.S. that were purchased in other regions, which underscores demand for the phone.

In a way, it makes sense that Motorola would be a bit conservative with its flagship strategy for traditional smartphones, given Samsung's dominance in North America with the Galaxy S series. Over the last few years, Motorola has focused on the Razr flip phones and, more recently, the Razr Fold, which consumers have received well. Only recently has Motorola begun adding top-tier chips to its Razr series.

But now, Motorola appears more confident in its premium smartphone offerings. Hagen tells me that last quarter, Motorola had its best quarter ever by revenue: "15% year over year, and the majority of that growth, of course, was driven by premium products." Clearly, there's a hunger for more high-end Motorola phones, and not just foldables.

What we know so far about the Motorola Signature 27

This year, Motorola skipped the higher-end Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, opting instead for the lower-end flagship chip on the Razr Fold. It still performs well, but based on what we know about the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the Signature 27 should be a powerful smartphone.

"What I'm most excited about is that the chipset is unlocking a few things for us," Hagen explains. That includes faster, more reliable performance, more helpful AI, and stronger connectivity. She highlights that "one of the big pillars for this franchise is an incredible camera system, both driven by hardware and software, with this common thread of needing to have an incredible global platform supporting it."

The Motorola Signature 27 comes with a few camera sensors, but has only disclosed the primary 50MP Sony Lytia 910 and the 200MP periscope telephoto lens.

She explains that when testing phones like the Signature 27, Motorola goes through several rounds with its own engineers and Qualcomm's engineers to fine-tune Snapdragon's image-processing AI and stabilization.

"We have a couple more rounds of work to do before, of course, we announce and launch the product. But we expect an exceptional DxO result that will help validate the overall experience."

In fact, she teases that even after one major round of camera testing, the Signature 27 is already proving to outperform the Razr Fold, which got high marks among foldable camera systems and has quickly become one of my favorite overall smartphone cameras.

Beyond the camera, Motorola is also partnering with Bang & Olufsen to enhance the audio experience. This multi-year partnership builds on Motorola's ongoing collaboration with Pantone and will bring B&O audio to Motorola's premium devices.

When asked why these partnerships matter, Hagen says Motorola doesn't have an ego and knows it doesn't have to do everything itself.

"We aim to partner with best-in-class partners that we know do it the best, and then partner with them and leverage their strong capabilities. It enables us to bring better capabilities to our end users more quickly."

As for what B&O brings to the table, "Obviously, they're a premium brand. They've been around for over 100 years, and they are able to help us through in the same way that we're doing the tuning on the back end with the camera. We're doing the exact same thing for sound."

New Moto, who dis?

A new chip, exceptional cameras, and a B&O partnership all come together to create a premium experience, but it also needs a premium design. This year, Motorola is switching up its design language to something that I originally found divisive.

The Motorola Signature 27 has a top-mounted camera housing with five distinct circles making up its camera sensors and a flash unit. I'm not gonna lie, when I first saw the Signature 27, it triggered a sense of tryptophobia that I haven't felt since the Nokia 9 PureView. But the more I look at it, the more I like it, and Hagen says there were some internal debates about how the cameras should be arranged.

"As you can imagine, this was a very popular one for internal debate, and everyone had their own subjective opinion," she explained.

"In some cases, many of the designs....kind of lean maybe into one specific gender. This one resonated with both."

One good thing about the camera housing (something we can all agree on) is that it doesn't protrude from one side of the phone, as Motorola phones have done over the past several years. As Hagen highlights, it's very balanced, not just visually, but physically. "There's no teeter-totter back and forth, and that was very, very well received."

The phone comes in two colorways: a grippy, black woven texture and a soft, green brushed textile-inspired finish. I didn't get to hold the phone, since it's not 100% final yet, but the Pantone Coal Smoke looked great, and the phone is quite thin, with premium-looking buttons on the frame. The camera housing also features two different textures: ceramic and brushed aluminum, for a very distinctive look.

Then, there's the name. In recent years, Motorola's naming convention in North America has included the full year after the product name, but this year it's simplified to the last two digits. It's a small change, but it's reminiscent of what Samsung does with the Galaxy S series, and I think it should resonate more with consumers.

In fact, Hagen says Motorola looked to competitors and the automotive industry for inspiration for the new naming scheme.

"We wanted something that was simple, clear, and easy to understand," Hagen told me. "Because the purpose of a generation is to indicate newness to folks that are considering a new product. To make it clear, as consumers are trying to, at or post-purchase, buy an accessory that will be compatible."

More to come... soon

The Motorola Signature 27 is launching globally this year, and while Motorola is remaining tight-lipped about the launch date and additional specs, it's clear that Hagen and company are very excited about the device.

"When I said on stage the other day that this is the best device that we've ever created... it truly is. The hardware specs are top-notch; the latest and greatest technology. And I think even more importantly, the outcomes and the experience that our users are going to have will really bring the product forward."
item.description: With the Motorola Signature 27, you no longer have to opt for a foldable to get the best Moto experience, and I couldn't be more excited.

item.title: Motorola just gave privacy fans a big reason to consider the Signature 27
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Motorola's Signature 27 will be one of the first phones powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.
  • GrapheneOS has confirmed initial support for the Signature 27, expanding beyond Google Pixel phones for the first time.
  • GrapheneOS is based on AOSP but focuses heavily on privacy, with optional Google Play services running sandboxed.

Motorola's Signature 27 is shaping up to be a serious contender for one of the best Android phones of the year. But beyond all the top-tier specs Motorola is packing into the phone, one of the most interesting features just confirmed for the Signature 27 is support for GrapheneOS.

At the Qualcomm Snapdragon Summit 2026, Motorola took to the stage to showcase one of the first smartphones powered by the new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. Qualcomm's new flagship chip is built on a 2nm process and can reach clock speeds of up to 5GHz, and the Signature 27 will be one of the first phones to use it.

The phone also breaks away from Motorola's previous Signature design with a new camera layout and packs plenty of other high-end features, including Audio by B&O. But alongside all those beastly specs, there's another interesting detail about the Signature 27, and that's support for GrapheneOS.

If you're unfamiliar, GrapheneOS is a privacy-focused take on Android that has grown significantly in popularity over the past few years. It's based on the Android Open Source Project, or AOSP, but is built with a much heavier focus on privacy and security and doesn't come with Google's services deeply integrated into the operating system.

You can still install Google Play services if you want, but they run sandboxed like regular apps rather than having the deeper system-level access they typically have on Android. Think of it as a much more privacy-focused version of Android that gives you greater control over how much access Google and other services have to your device.

Historically, GrapheneOS has officially supported only Google Pixel devices because of the project's strict hardware and security requirements. But that's finally changing, with the Motorola Signature 27 set to become one of the first non-Pixel smartphones to receive official GrapheneOS support.

GrapheneOS confirmed on X that initial support is planned for the Signature 27, although it stopped short of revealing many more details. We don't yet know exactly when support will arrive or what the installation process will look like, but we now know that Signature 27 owners will have the option to run GrapheneOS.

Motorola hasn't announced the exact release date or pricing for the Signature 27 just yet. But between the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the new flagship hardware, and now official GrapheneOS support, Motorola is certainly giving Android enthusiasts another reason to keep an eye on this phone.
item.description: Motorola' Signature 27 just got way more interesting, thanks to official GrapheneOS support

item.title: Google Photos update packs a handful of vintage styles with 'Moods' and curated wardrobes
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Google Photos rolls out an update to help users edit their summer photos, as "Moods" gets introduced.
  • With "Moods," users will find a selection of vintage styles that "automatically adapt" to your photo, solidifying Google's intent of a feature that's more than a simple filter.
  • This update also brings Gemini Spark integration, giving users an easier, prompt-based way of editing their photos and removing unwanted guests.

Google Photos is rolling out a few updates to help immortalize the pictures we've taken throughout the summer. The app receives a new set of filters, as well as additional AI assistance.

Today (Sept. 24), Google detailed an update for the Photos app that begins with Gemini Spark integration. Availability is rolling out for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S. The company says users can "brighten and share" photos using a single prompt with Gemini Spark. What's more, users can remove people from the photo's background, leaving those who matter.

This update is also introducing "Moods." Google says Moods brings styles that users can use to edit their photos. However, it adds that these are "more than filters." You'll find a few options such as 35mm film and 2000s digicam. When you apply a style, Google states Moods will "automatically adapt" to your photo. But users can take things a step further.

You'll find sliders to fine-tune how much a style influences your photo, as well as mixing themes from other styles. Moods are rolling out to Android users globally.

The Google Photos app is upgrading its markup tool in this September patch. The tool now provides a "redact pen" to help users blur sensitive details. Additionally, you'll find "precise thickness sliders for custom sketches and fresh fonts to make your text pop." Another new addition involves the app's Remix templates. Google is rolling out 15 Remix templates that turn your photos into photo booth-style shots, birthday cards, and more.

The redact pen and other markup tool updates are arriving to Android users globally. The additional Remix templates are arriving for Android and iOS users over 18 in "select countries."

Google detailed one final update, but it's more of an expansion. The Photos app's Wardrobe feature, which lets users curate a digital closet for clothing styles, is now rolling out in the U.S., India, and Brazil on Android and iOS.

Expanding features

Android Central's Take

Regarding the app's Wardrobe feature, I can't help but think of what my colleague Jay said, "If your closet is so messy that only machine learning can sort it out, maybe the real answer is to spend twenty minutes folding clothes." I can't help but agree. I can see the appeal behind this feature. It's easy to quickly visualize things without dipping in and out and trying things on. But... why does this computer need to know the clothes I have?

If you remember Moto's Razr reveal earlier this year, Wardrobe in Photos would sound familiar. The feature evolves the static gallery into a personal stylist and daily content hub. Wardrobe can automatically identify specific pieces of clothing, helping you fill out your digital closet. Users can mix and match different outfits and share those with others. So if you're looking to coordinate fits for your next outing, this might help.

Gemini Spark is a proactive AI that Google launched in May. The AI is capable of managing tasks and workflows in the background without disturbing you. Users can think of Spark as an AI agent that gets the dirty work done for you. If connected, you can bring Gemini Spark into your Gmail, Docs, Slides, and other apps. You can automate tasks with Gemini Spark or review meeting and email summaries.

item.title: I played with Meta's new AI gaming engine reboot and can't believe how far it's come
item.dc:content:
Imagine you're scrolling through your Instagram or Facebook feed and see an ad for a game. I get these all the time and they usually catch my interest, but instead of just being a video to watch, what if the game was fully playable right inside your feed?

That's exactly what Meta is working on right now with Horizon Create, a total reboot of the company's Horizon Worlds platform that puts Meta's ubiquitous AI presense at the very heart of its brand new gaming engine.

I sat down with four members of the development team at Meta Connect 2026 as they both demonstrated the new tech to me and let me toy around with it myself, and I came away impressed.

Create what you imagine

Back in the day, I put quite a bit of time into Farmville. It was one of those weird guilty pleasures that was more enjoyable with friends, and it helped that it was built conveninetly into Facebook on my PC. I can't I've been quite as interested in "social media gaming" since then, though.

But Meta's new Horizon Worlds reboot is sparking an interest I had long forgotten about, and it all starts with how easy it is to make something. Like a normal AI prompt, you can start your first game with just a simple idea. Meta showed me a handful, but the one that triggered my imagination the most was creating an adventure game like Fable.

My demo began on Meta's Horizon Create smartphone app, which showed an Instagram-like gaming feed. Scrolling through the feed pulled up dozens of different games, from adventure titles to zombie survival games, crafting titles, you name it. Each one of these can be played instantly by just tapping it, and some of them even let you remix them, but I'll cover that in a moment.

While these games are AI-generated, they don't quite fit into the "slop" category that you might immediately think of. Everything in Horizon Create starts with a prompt, but the engine supports asset imports (so developers can bring in their own models and audio), and you can move, adjust, scale, or remix objects to your heart's content.

What's particularly amazing is that you can create things with friends, all while playing in the game world at the same time. During my demo, we had five people in the same world, all tasked with different jobs. One person was working on the weather, one was working on ground objects, another was working on building vehicles, and I was just running around shooting things.

I was also able to tap on any created object and freely adjust its size and position in the world, plus ask Meta AI to change the object in any way I could think of. Better yet, once things looked good, publishing it to Facebook, Instagram, or Horizon took just two taps.

This is a huge departure from current mobile game development concepts, even if you use AI like Claude to code something like a Roblox game. While Claude can be brilliant at coding, it can't do everything for you. I've tried my hand at making a few apps and almost always run into a wall because I'm simply not a coder.

Meta Horizon Create works fully in-engine and doesn't require 3rd party tools or SDKs to work. That means you don't have to use another AI agent and wait for things to happen; all prompts and changes happen in real-time as you're in the game, and it's pretty crazy to watch.

The desktop Horizon Studio app delivers even more options, as well. You can look at the entire development tree, including dependencies, delve down into each of the game's mechanics, and more. All of these can be iterated on, and it was pretty wild to see it all in action.

Meta has been working on this new version of Horizon only since April, so while this all seems extremely advanced, it's surprisingly early in development. They're expecting it to start rolling out early next year, but you can sign up to test out the new platform right now.
item.description: Facebook games are getting a massive level-up with Meta Horizon Create and Horizon Studio, and they'll be playable straight from your feed.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Sutrich
item.dc:description: <p>Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Because of this, he covers both smartphones and VR technology, two avenues that split his passions right down the middle. From Nokia fan to Android fanatic, Nick has been writing about and reviewing smartphones since 2011. An avid gamer and equally well-versed tech head, Nick worked in the IT industry for 15 years, helping to further develop his technical knowledge, which has become particularly important in his fight with PWM sensitivity and deep dives into display technology. He's a huge fan of any phone that can fold in half and loves getting into the nitty-gritty with folding phone coverage for the site. He's also got over a decade of experience with VR gaming, having used the original Oculus DK1 and every major VR headset since then, passionately covering Android Central's Meta Quest content and smart glasses coverage with his weekly thVRsday column on Thursdays. Beyond that, you'll find Nick taking photos of anything and everything, from the beautiful mountains of his home to the chickens in his backyard, and using them to compare cameras to help you choose the best one.</p>

item.title: Even Realities' 'Exposed' won't sugarcoat smart glasses in micro-drama series about Meta privacy concerns
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Even Realities introduced its "Exposed" campaign, which will evolve into an eight-episode micro-drama on TikTok on October 8.
  • "Exposed" will shine a bright light on the privacy concerns that smart glasses with cameras bring to the world.
  • Consent is key, but when someone can walk around with a pair of glasses that's capturing you, the drama will ask: where's the consent in that?
  • "Exposed" is directed by Ishana Night Shyamalan, alongside VITURE Worldwide.

Even Realities looks to capitalize on Meta Connect by introducing its "Exposed" campaign. The microdrama draws awareness to the ongoing issue we're already facing: the extreme privacy concerns regarding camera-equipped smart glasses.

In a press release, Even Realities says its micro-drama explores the impacts these types of devices have on the people around us. Deepa Patel, managing director at VITURE Worldwide, said, “We didn’t want to run another traditional ad that people instantly skip; we wanted to, as always, tap into a cultural conversation and build a piece of entertainment genuinely worth watching.”

Cameras are moving away from our phones, and that's what Even Realities wants to spotlight. "Exposed" is also a part of VICE Media and is rolling out across major cities like the San Francisco Bay Area and New York this week before an eight-episode micro-drama begins on October 8. Even Realities says the reality is simple: "smart glasses do not need cameras to be useful..."

Consent is huge. And in a world where we have smart glasses with cameras, anyone can be captured and recorded at any time. The "Exposed" campaign and micro-drama is directed by Ishana Night Shyamalan, and it's already getting its name out there in big places. Even Realities states it's running the campaign in Times Square in New York with the intent of bringing ads to more private places: bathrooms and gyms.

In San Francisco, the company has brought its campaign to buses running around Meta's campus in time for its Connect event. When the full eight-episode series launches on October 8, you can catch them on TikTok.

Meta Connect continues, but let's not forget...

Meta Connect is continuing as usual this year, despite the many alarms raised about smart glasses (or "pervert glasses" insult). It's forced Meta to take a step back and rethink some of its products. On one hand, we have rumors that the company is experimenting with a hardware lock for cameras and microphones. On the other hand, we have reports that the camera would disable if the LED indicator had been tampered with.

All of this is in response to users not wanting to be filmed or captured constantly by someone's smart glasses. It's a privacy violation, and when bad apples mess with the LED indicator, you're really in the dark. Meta did reveal some glasses—the Ray-Ban Audio—at Connect 2026 without a camera, but there are still plenty with one. However, VITURE's founders have revealed glasses with a privacy feature we wish everyone else would adopt.

Android Central's Take

I think I can already imagine where Even Realities' "Exposed" micro-drama is headed. It makes sense. And for people who will watch it, it might change their perspective. Sure, there's the usefulness of having these glasses with a camera. It's another way of recording memories. However, there's a malicious undertone to this. There's the ease for someone with nefarious intentions to capture you and do... what with it? I'd have to agree: smart glasses can be just as useful without a camera that's capturing people without their consent or knowledge.

A post shared by Even Realities (@evenrealities)

A photo posted by

item.title: Pixel Watch is getting blood pressure tracking and new health tools this week
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • The Google Health app is rolling out blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality tracking to its Health Guardian suite.
  • The features analyze long-term pattern changes over weeks rather than providing instant clinical readings, functioning as wellness indicators instead of direct medical diagnostic tools.
  • The update is available for free to Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 users, while Fitbit Air owners can access it via a Google Health Premium subscription.

Google is expanding the health-monitoring tools available on its Pixel Watch lineup, with three new Health Guardian features starting to roll out this week. The update adds blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality metrics to the Google Health app.

The features are intended to look for changes over time, not to replace traditional medical measurements. Pixel Watch owners can start to set them up this week, Google says.

According to the tech giant, the Health Guardian system uses AI models trained on billions of minutes of sensor data to recognize subtle physiological patterns, so the watch can estimate trends from signals it already collects without a dedicated blood-pressure cuff or blood sample.

That approach is especially notable for trends in insulin resistance, which Google says can analyze multiple weeks of physiological data without requiring a blood draw. The company says the feature is meant to promote overall wellness, not to diagnose diabetes or replace clinical testing.

The additions join Google's broader Health Guardian suite, which also includes Breathing Emergency Detection on the Pixel Watch 4 and Watch 5 in select European countries.

Existing owners also get in on the fun, as the new tools will be offered for free on the Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5. Users of the Fitbit Air will soon have access as part of a Google Health Premium subscription.

The first detailed trend reports are expected in early October, offering users their first real glimpse at how Google’s trend-based health monitoring functions outside of the company’s launch messaging.

item.title: Amazon forgot it's not Prime Day yet and slashed 53% off the Fire HD 10 tablet
item.dc:content:
Amazon doesn't refresh its tablets and e-readers every year because it doesn't need to. The Kindle tablet series is wildly popular year round, because there's no other brand delivering such value-packed products at prices as low as Amazon. What's even more awesome is that Amazon is kicking off a few October Prime Day deals ahead of Big Deal Days, slashing more than half off the Fire HD 10 (2023) tablet.

Retailing for $154.99, the Fire HD 10 was already an insanely cheap 10-inch tablet. This 53% discount chops it down to an unbelievably low $72.99 on Amazon, but only for a limited time. The large 10.1-inch Full HD LCD display with a crisp 1920 x 1200 resolution makes this an ideal tablet for adults as well as children, which is why we named it the best cheap Android tablet for kids in 2026.

  • Prime Big Deal Days returns October 6-7: see the full list of early deals

Amazon Fire HD 10 tablet (2023): $149.99 $72.99 at Amazon

The Amazon Fire HD 10 tablet has a lovely 10.1-inch screen, expandable storage, a long-lasting battery, and front and rear cameras, easily making it one of Amazon's most premium tablets. At more than half off its usual price, you won't find anything remotely close to this performance level for just $70 and some pocket change.View Deal

✅Recommended if: you want a cheap Amazon Fire tablet below $100 for streaming, gaming, or as a shared smart display for a family household; you need something with a battery life of over 12 hours; you want something that includes expandable storage.

❌Skip this deal if: you prefer a thin and lightweight build; you need higher quality cameras.

Although this deal is for the 32GB version of the device, the Fire HD 10 supports expandable storage via microSD, and you can add up to 1TB of storage. The uptime is superb, giving you about 13 hours of battery life per charge, and there are 5MP cameras on both the front and rear that are good enough for basic needs like video calls.

The tablet has easy-to-use parental controls for shared device usage and is compatible with the separately sold Amazon stylus.

One of the Fire HD 10's rarer features is the 3.5mm audio jack, allowing you to plug in headphones. It also sports dual stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos, so the auditory experience when streaming your favorite TV shows or movies is fabulous.

The Amazon tablet is powered by an octa-core processor and 4GB RAM, which may not sound like much, but actually manages to perform well in real life. In fact, you'll be delightfully taken aback by how decently the Amazon Fire HD 10 2023 handles multitasking, light office work, and even some gaming.
item.description: This deal won't last forever, so if you've been wanting a 10-inch tablet for streaming shows and music or casual gaming, now is your chance.

item.dc:creator: Namerah Saud Fatmi
item.dc:description: <p>Namerah Saud Fatmi has been interested in technology ever since the days of the OG Razr Flip and back when the PlayStation Portable was the sickest console to have ever existed. Having fiddled with gadgets, PC parts, and techy tidbits since her early tweens, Namerah started sharing her expertise and opinions with the world in late 2018. Fast forward to today and she has grown into an even more curious — and seasoned — tech enthusiast with a penchant for experimenting with accessories, phones, and mobile devices. Her coverage as a Senior Editor at Android Central focuses on the world of mobile phone accessories, occasionally branching out into sects like gaming, software, hardware, and more. Before becoming a full-time writer for Android Central, Namerah was a freelance writer with bylines at other respectable publications such as XDA Developers, Neowin, and Good e-Reader. She also helps out Android Central's sister brands Windows Central and iMore on and off. Namerah is based out of Malaysia, where she lives with her four-legged life partner, a black cat named Bruce Wayne. Her hobbies include casual gaming, attempting to pet anything classified as an animal, chugging coffee, traveling profusely, and going on culinary adventures whenever possible.</p>

✅Recommended if: you want a cheap Amazon Fire tablet below $100 for streaming, gaming, or as a shared smart display for a family household; you need something with a battery life of over 12 hours; you want something that includes expandable storage.

❌Skip this deal if: you prefer a thin and lightweight build; you need higher quality cameras.

Although this deal is for the 32GB version of the device, the Fire HD 10 supports expandable storage via microSD, and you can add up to 1TB of storage. The uptime is superb, giving you about 13 hours of battery life per charge, and there are 5MP cameras on both the front and rear that are good enough for basic needs like video calls.

The tablet has easy-to-use parental controls for shared device usage and is compatible with the separately sold Amazon stylus.

One of the Fire HD 10's rarer features is the 3.5mm audio jack, allowing you to plug in headphones. It also sports dual stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos, so the auditory experience when streaming your favorite TV shows or movies is fabulous.

The Amazon tablet is powered by an octa-core processor and 4GB RAM, which may not sound like much, but actually manages to perform well in real life. In fact, you'll be delightfully taken aback by how decently the Amazon Fire HD 10 2023 handles multitasking, light office work, and even some gaming.

item.title: Best Buy will give you a free pair of wireless earbuds with your Googlebook preorder — here's the deal
item.dc:content:
It's official: the Googlebook is coming, and while this laptop isn't receiving as many preorder deals as, say, a new Android phone might, there is one offer that you should know about. Preorder one of the new laptops ahead of their October 4th release date and Best Buy will give you a free pair of Google Pixel Buds 2a (in Hazel), no strings attached. There's also some trade-in credit up for grabs if you have an old laptop lying around.

Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo are all launching their Googlebooks on the aforementioned date, and this preorder deal from Best Buy presents an easy way to get equipped with two pieces of Pixel tech in one fell swoop. Now if they'll just throw in a free Google Pixel phone, it will really be a party...

Get a FREE pair of Google Pixel Buds 2a with any Googlebook preorder at Best Buy

The Googlebook finally arrives in the US on October 4th, and Best Buy will give you a free pair of Pixel Buds 2a when you preorder one of the laptops on its site. That's a $120 value, no strings attached! These budget-friendly earbuds by Google feature customizable sound with solid noise cancellation and up to 20 hours of battery life on a single charge (with the included charging case).

Starting at $899, your Googlebook preorder also comes with three free months of YouTube Premium and Adobe Photoshop, in addition to 12 months of Google AI Pro and 5TB of cloud storage. View Deal

What is a Googlebook?

Designed as a successor to Chromebooks, Googlebooks are laptops built for integration into the modern AI-focused device ecosystem. These premium laptops feature touchscreen displays with great battery life (up to 14 hours) and the latest processors from Intel and Qualcomm, plus you'll get to experience a ton of new software features that seamlessly connect the Googlebook with your Android phone.

Other specs include backlit keyboards, convertible designs, and 16GB of RAM out of the box. Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo are all participating in the initial Googlebook launch, with devices that range from $899 to $1,299 for OLED models. In addition to the free wireless earbuds, your preorder will come with free limited subscriptions to YouTube Premium, Adobe Premiere, and Google AI Pro subscriptions.
item.description: Preorder the new Googlebook from Best Buy and you'll get a free pair of Pixel Buds 2a with your purchase.

He’s particularly passionate about eliminating buyer’s remorse and taking subjects that can be confusing for shoppers — such as switching wireless carriers or buying a new smart TV — and breaking them down into simple, easy-to-understand terms. Whether you’re a veteran tech-head or a novice, Patrick offers honest, no-nonsense shopping advice with years of hands-on experience to back it up. When he isn’t hunting down the best discounts or digging through the fine print of a carrier deal, Patrick enjoys trekking around the Rocky Mountains, camping out at a brewery, or spending time with his beloved polydactyl cat. &nbsp;</p>

item.title: Pixel 11's newest trick is calling local businesses so you don't have to
item.dc:content:
What you need to know

  • Pixel 11 users can now delegate routine calls — like checking store inventory, booking appointments, or changing reservations — directly to Gemini.
  • You can monitor the entire conversation via a live transcript on your screen and take over the call at any moment.
  • The preview begins September 24 for Gemini paid subscribers in the Phone by Google Public Beta.

Google today introduced a new task for Gemini on the Pixel 11: helping you dodge those pesky calls you keep putting off. The company is testing a feature that allows Gemini to contact businesses for routine tasks such as checking inventory, booking appointments, and changing reservations.

The idea builds on Google’s existing Hold for Me and Direct My Call features, which already take care of parts of the experience of a phone call. This time, Gemini goes one step further. You tell it what you need, and it will call the business, identify itself, go through automated menus, wait on hold, and speak with the person who answers, all through the Gemini app.

Google’s updated terms say these agentic calls are placed from your own phone number and use an AI-generated voice. That makes the feature less like a glorified voicemail assistant and more like an AI impersonating you.

You aren't handing over the phone altogether, though. The experience will include a live transcript so you can follow the conversation as it happens, Google says. If Gemini starts to go off the rails, you can take over the call at any point.

Google says it’s limiting the initial rollout as it works through the nuances of real-world conversations. There’s a good practical reason for Google’s decision to limit the initial rollout. These are conversations that are real. Gemini's calls are from real customers trying to book appointments, hold items, or change the date of services, meaning that businesses and the people who work for them have to deal with the AI on the other end.

The preview starts on September 24 for Gemini paid subscribers enrolled in the Phone by Google Public Beta, which is limited to Pixel 11 phones in the U.S.
item.description: Google's new Pixel feature brings us one step closer to never talking on the phone again.

item.title: This Pixel 11 setting fixed my biggest issue with modern smartphone photography
item.dc:content:
Have you ever taken a photo on your phone, only to look back later and wonder where all the life went? I've seen people ask why their newer smartphone photos look dull and sterile compared to their older phone, and the answer mainly lies in how phones process photos these days.

Google seems to have heard everyone's cries and implemented a new feature on the Pixel 11 series called Camera Looks. These looks are more than a plain filter; they change how color science works and how shadows are calculated when you take a photo, leading to a result you'll hopefully like better.

What are Camera Looks?

To understand what Camera Looks does to your photos, you first have to understand how modern smartphone photography works. Unlike a "normal" camera, modern smartphones don't just take one picture when you tap the shutter button. Instead, your Pixel phone constantly takes pictures while the camera viewfinder is open; it just doesn't store them until you tap the shutter button.

The moment you press the shutter button, your Pixel saves roughly five photos taken before you press it, plus another five taken during and slightly after. Each photo is taken at different exposure values — meaning some photos are darker while others are brighter — to ensure the camera captures the widest range of light in an image. All this happens in less than a split second.

Your Pixel then takes those photos and combines them into a single picture at the pixel level. If you've ever taken a photo and then immediately tapped the thumbnail to see your shot, you've probably seen the picture "pop" into place and look a lot better after a second or two. This is the result of what Google calls HDR+.

While brightening the shadows and reducing the brightest parts of the photos might be technically excellent, it doesn't look "correct" to our eyes. After years of developing HDR+ into the industry's most technically advanced photo-processing software, Google is letting users pull back on the proverbial reins if they want to.

Google calls this extra control "Camera Looks," and it gives users a quick, easy way to make the Pixel camera look and work the way they want. You can reduce or enhance any specific processing parameters, including sharpening, shadows, vibrance, tinting, and more.

Camera Looks aren't "filters." Each look changes how the photo is processed when taken and delivers a different end look. A filter is something applied to a photo after it's taken, while Camera Looks changes the entire processing pipeline.

How to use Camera Looks on a Pixel 11

Camera Looks is supported on all Pixel 11 series phones, including the base Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google hasn't ported this feature to older Pixel phones yet, as Camera Looks currently runs at the hardware level on the Tensor G6's ISP.

Camera Looks is a simple feature on the surface, but it also lets power users dive into more granular settings. Here's how to apply basic Camera Looks to your photos:

1. Open the camera app. You can also double-press the power button to quickly launch the camera.

2. Tap the Settings Sliders button on the bottom right of the viewfinder.

3. Tap on the Looks button on the bottom left of the viewfinder.

4. The viewfinder will now transform into a series of cards. At the top, tap the dropdown next to "default look" and select your desired base processing style.

5. You can also swipe through the Camera Looks cards to choose from 7 different preset options.

Setting your look as the default

By default, you'll need to tap the Camera Looks button every time you reopen the camera. Google does this to make "normal" photo-taking easy, but you can also set your preferred camera look as the default when you open the camera. To do that, follow these steps:

1. Open the camera app.

2. Tap the photo settings icon on the bottom left. It looks like a gear.

3. Tap the More button on the top right of the pop-up. It looks like three dots.

4. Scroll down and enable Always use selected look.

Now, when you open your Pixel's camera, the Camera Look you previously configured will always be enabled. To disable it, just tap the Camera Look button on the bottom right, then swipe through the cards to select another look.

Getting the most out of Camera Looks

While the carousel of cards is a quick way to get some nice presets, Camera Looks lets you dial in eight different properties of the Pixel's photography engine and adjust them in granular detail. When you open Camera Looks, you'll see a row of buttons along the bottom for individual settings. Here's what each one does:

Contrast (-10 to +10): The difference between the image's brightest and darkest parts. Increase this number to create starker darks and lights, and lower it to make the image gentler.

Highlights (-10 to +10): This refers to the brightest parts of a photo, usually something like sunlight coming through a window, a reflection in glass, etc. Increase this number to brighten highlights, and decrease it to reduce them.

Shadows (-10 to +10): This setting affects the darkest parts of a photo. Increasing this number brightens all the dark parts in an image. Decreasing this number will make the darker parts even darker, resulting in higher-contrast scenes.

Vibrance (-10 to +10): This setting affects color intensity. Higher vibrance settings make colors "pop" but can look unrealistic or cartoony at too-high settings. Lower settings make colors look duller.

Tint (-10 to +10): Adjusts how green or magenta an image is. Higher numbers skew the image toward a more magenta tone, while lower numbers make the image look greener.

Warmth (-10 to +10): Adjusts how blue or yellow an image is. Higher numbers skew the image toward yellow, or warmer colors, while lower numbers skew the image toward blue, or cooler tones.

Sharpness (0 to 15): This refers to how much artificial sharpening is added to a photo. Digital photography often uses sharpening to make photos look "high resolution" by enhancing fine detail, but an image that's too sharp looks noticeably fake and often "harsh."

Grain (None/Weak/Moderate/Strong): Adds an artificial grain look to photos. This differs from digital noise, a by-product of how digital photo sensors work. The grain setting does not enhance fine detail. It only adds a grain filter.

Feel free to play with each of these settings to find the look you want. If you don't like the look of stock Pixel photos, I suggest adjusting three settings right away: shadows, vibrance, and sharpness.

Try dropping the shadows a notch or two and see if you like the look. I think the preset "Shadows" Look (found in the drop-down menu at the top of the viewfinder when Camera Looks is enabled) already does a good job of adjusting this setting.

When you're done with that, try giving vibrance a little punch-up. Start with +2 and adjust from there. That, combined with shadow darkening, should give your Pixel photos a nice pop. Lastly, try reducing sharpness just a bit by bringing it down to 8 (the default is 10). This will reduce sharpening, making the photo look more like film and less digital.
item.description: Modern smartphone photography can look flat and sterile, but the Pixel 11's Camera Looks feature helps solve that problem.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Sutrich
item.dc:description: <p>Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Because of this, he covers both smartphones and VR technology, two avenues that split his passions right down the middle. From Nokia fan to Android fanatic, Nick has been writing about and reviewing smartphones since 2011. An avid gamer and equally well-versed tech head, Nick worked in the IT industry for 15 years, helping to further develop his technical knowledge, which has become particularly important in his fight with PWM sensitivity and deep dives into display technology. He's a huge fan of any phone that can fold in half and loves getting into the nitty-gritty with folding phone coverage for the site. He's also got over a decade of experience with VR gaming, having used the original Oculus DK1 and every major VR headset since then, passionately covering Android Central's Meta Quest content and smart glasses coverage with his weekly thVRsday column on Thursdays. Beyond that, you'll find Nick taking photos of anything and everything, from the beautiful mountains of his home to the chickens in his backyard, and using them to compare cameras to help you choose the best one.</p>

item.title: These $40 flat-head earbuds reminded me of the '90s in the best possible way
item.dc:content:
I have fond memories of using flat-head earbuds as a kid in the '90s; I was just getting started with music discovery, and I was basically glued to my Walkman. I still use earbuds today, whether it's Bluetooth products like the FoKus Amadeus, Bose QuietComfort Ultra Gen 2, Status Pro X, or IEMs such as the Fiio FX15, Thieaudio Monarch MKIV, and Elysian Acoustic Labs Pilgrim.

So when Sivga said it's coming out with flat-head buds, I was obviously interested. The M260 have a bland naming convention (in a sense, that fits its retro positioning), but that's thankfully the only negative thing I have to say about these buds. They cost $39 on Amazon and come with a standard 3.5mm connector, and you can also get a USB-C version (like I did) when you buy at Sivga's website (these are $40 as well).

Let's start with the design. The M260 may be aimed at the budget category, but they're made out of machined aluminum, and the build quality is exquisite. The silver finish looks great in its own right, and the gold accents add a bit of flair.

There are a decent number of these earbuds around now, but they're mostly made out of plastic, and the attention to detail that Sivga lavished on the M260 makes the earbuds stand out quite a bit. This isn't anything new; I tested Sivga's Luan headset two years ago, and it has a delightful design and a high degree of comfort. It's so good that my wife immediately stole it to use with her gaming machine.

Anyway, the flat-head design of the M260 means they're extremely comfortable to wear, and if you've used IEMs in the past and didn't quite get a good fit, you should consider giving these a go. Unlike regular earbuds where the sound tube nuzzles into your ear canal — causing fatigue with long-term use — these buds sit around the outer ear, and they don't exert any pressure. You don't get a tight seal, so there isn't the same level of noise isolation as Bluetooth earbuds, but that isn't a big problem.

Most of the time, I didn't even realize I was wearing the buds, and they're designed for all-day use. The bundled ear tips provide good cushioning, and honestly, these may just be among the most comfortable earbuds I used in a long time. Also, they're just fun to use; I couldn't keep a smile off my face the entire time I used these.

Sivga went with a standard MMCX connector to plug the buds to the cable, and that means you can easily switch out cables should you need to do so. The bundled cable is of a decent quality, and it has a nylon sheath and a braided design that gives it better durability. Oh, and the cable gets inline controls, so you can easily adjust volume and pause/play music. It has a built-in mic as well, allowing you to take calls.

The USB-C model has a built-in DAC, and it is quite decent. I used the M260 with my Pixel 11 Pro XL, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Find X9 Ultra, and they did a great job with a diverse range of music. Sivga went with a custom 14.2mm dynamic driver, and it has a tight bass with a good rumble, clean mids, and smooth treble.

The mid-range is where these earbuds shine, with vocals coming through cleanly and with plenty of definition. They're a great choice if you want to listen to music or stream movies and TV shows.

Because they use USB-C, you can use the buds with just about any phone, tablet, and gaming console without having to get a dongle. That kind of convenience is a big deal in and of itself, and it's good to see Sivga provide a USB-C version.

Honestly, if you want earbuds you can plug in, you can't go wrong with the M260. They have a delightfully-retro design with unmatched comfort, great sound, and build quality that's guaranteed to last. Coming in at $40, they're a great value as well.
item.description: Sivga's M260 earbuds are full of nostalgic charm, and you get a modern driver with USB-C connectivity.
item.author: harish.jonnalagadda@futurenet.com (Harish Jonnalagadda)
item.dc:creator: Harish Jonnalagadda
item.dc:description: <p>Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing the mobile category. He started his tech journey at a very young age by tweaking Windows XP installations, and that hobby ignited an enthusiasm that led him into the world of PC modding. After picking up a Bachelor's degree in computer science, he decided to pursue his passion by covering PC hardware at VR-Zone, where he reviewed motherboards, video cards, and DRAM modules.</p><p><br>While he used iPhones initially, switching to the Nexus 4 served as the catalyst to explore Android's burgeoning ecosystem, and he pivoted to writing about mobile tech, joining Android Central's newsroom back in 2014. As a Senior Editor, he oversees the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, enthusiast audio products, networking hardware, and storage servers, leveraging his engineering background and extensive experience testing mobile hardware to evaluate the latest phones and accessories.<br></p><p>In over a decade of covering Android, he has used pretty much every single major phone released globally, giving him an unrivaled view into Google's mobile platform. media:content.media:description: Sivga M260 flat-head buds
media:content.media:text: Sivga M260 flat-head buds
media:content.media:title: Sivga M260 flat-head buds

item.content:encoded:
I have fond memories of using flat-head earbuds as a kid in the '90s; I was just getting started with music discovery, and I was basically glued to my Walkman. I still use earbuds today, whether it's Bluetooth products like the FoKus Amadeus, Bose QuietComfort Ultra Gen 2, Status Pro X, or IEMs such as the Fiio FX15, Thieaudio Monarch MKIV, and Elysian Acoustic Labs Pilgrim.

So when Sivga said it's coming out with flat-head buds, I was obviously interested. The M260 have a bland naming convention (in a sense, that fits its retro positioning), but that's thankfully the only negative thing I have to say about these buds. They cost $39 on Amazon and come with a standard 3.5mm connector, and you can also get a USB-C version (like I did) when you buy at Sivga's website (these are $40 as well).

Let's start with the design. The M260 may be aimed at the budget category, but they're made out of machined aluminum, and the build quality is exquisite. The silver finish looks great in its own right, and the gold accents add a bit of flair.

There are a decent number of these earbuds around now, but they're mostly made out of plastic, and the attention to detail that Sivga lavished on the M260 makes the earbuds stand out quite a bit. This isn't anything new; I tested Sivga's Luan headset two years ago, and it has a delightful design and a high degree of comfort. It's so good that my wife immediately stole it to use with her gaming machine.

Anyway, the flat-head design of the M260 means they're extremely comfortable to wear, and if you've used IEMs in the past and didn't quite get a good fit, you should consider giving these a go. Unlike regular earbuds where the sound tube nuzzles into your ear canal — causing fatigue with long-term use — these buds sit around the outer ear, and they don't exert any pressure. You don't get a tight seal, so there isn't the same level of noise isolation as Bluetooth earbuds, but that isn't a big problem.

Most of the time, I didn't even realize I was wearing the buds, and they're designed for all-day use. The bundled ear tips provide good cushioning, and honestly, these may just be among the most comfortable earbuds I used in a long time. Also, they're just fun to use; I couldn't keep a smile off my face the entire time I used these.

Sivga went with a standard MMCX connector to plug the buds to the cable, and that means you can easily switch out cables should you need to do so. The bundled cable is of a decent quality, and it has a nylon sheath and a braided design that gives it better durability. Oh, and the cable gets inline controls, so you can easily adjust volume and pause/play music. It has a built-in mic as well, allowing you to take calls.

The USB-C model has a built-in DAC, and it is quite decent. I used the M260 with my Pixel 11 Pro XL, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Find X9 Ultra, and they did a great job with a diverse range of music. Sivga went with a custom 14.2mm dynamic driver, and it has a tight bass with a good rumble, clean mids, and smooth treble.

The mid-range is where these earbuds shine, with vocals coming through cleanly and with plenty of definition. They're a great choice if you want to listen to music or stream movies and TV shows.

Because they use USB-C, you can use the buds with just about any phone, tablet, and gaming console without having to get a dongle. That kind of convenience is a big deal in and of itself, and it's good to see Sivga provide a USB-C version.

Honestly, if you want earbuds you can plug in, you can't go wrong with the M260. They have a delightfully-retro design with unmatched comfort, great sound, and build quality that's guaranteed to last. Coming in at $40, they're a great value as well.

item.title: 5 things I learned after a month of daily-driving the Pixel 11 Pro XL
item.dc:content:
It's been a month of using the Pixel 11 Pro XL as my daily driver, and I generally like what Google did with the device this year. There are some frustrations (just like with every phone I test), but as a whole, the Pixel 11 Pro XL is better than its predecessors, and while I don't necessarily like Google's aggressive stance on AI, all of these features are easy enough to ignore.

Instead of a traditional long-term review, I wanted to highlight five things that stood out the most in the month I used the Pixel 11 Pro XL, so let's get started.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL can take a beating

The Pixel 11 Pro XL doesn't look too different to the 10 Pro XL, and I don't mind that one bit. The design is visually distinctive, and I like how clean and minimal the camera visor looks this year. The Obsidian model doesn't have much flair (you'll need to buy the Canyon instead), but the all-matte texture feels great to hold and use.

The positioning of the camera bar means there's no wobble at all when using the phone on a table — this is diametrically opposite to Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra, which wobbles if you look at it. It is on the heavier side at 226g, but the weight is balanced well, and at no point did I feel that it was unwieldy to use.

I'm pleased to report that the phone has proven durability. The Pixel 11 Pro XL took over a dozen tumbles in the month I used it, and while there is some visible damage on the sides, it is all around the mid-frame, and the glass panels at the front and rear are unharmed. There was one notable instance where it skid face-down on a tiled floor; it just slid out of my hand, and my rescue attempt ended up with me kicking it across the room. Anyway, outside of minor scratching on one edge of the screen, the panel held up admirably.

It's good to see that Google actually paid quite a bit of attention to build quality, as the Pixel 11 Pro XL is designed to last a better part of a decade. I had issues with the fit and finish of older Pixels, but that thankfully hasn't been the case in the last two years, so it looks like Google finally has a handle on this.

The cameras are good — if not the best you'll find

I went to an Apple briefing to go hands-on with the iPhone Duo, and normally, I use whatever phone I'm daily driving to take product photos. In this scenario, it was the Pixel 11 Pro XL, and after taking two photos, I realized I made a mistake.

It took significantly more effort to shoot with the Pixel 11 Pro XL, and I wasn't satisfied with the resultant imagery — so much so that I regretted not bringing the Find X9 Ultra at least a half-dozen times. This isn't to say that the cameras are bad on the Pixel 11 Pro XL; if anything, the phone does a better job than previous years. I got plenty of great shots out of the camera over the last month, but it isn't well-suited to take product photos in questionable lighting.

Chinese flagships like the Find X9 Ultra, X9 Pro, Vivo X300 Ultra, X300 Pro, and the Xiaomi 17 Ultra do such a good job in this area that I didn't spot the Pixel 11 Pro XL's obvious limitations with the sensor size and resolution. Anyway, I got usable shots (if not the best quality or detail), but it reinforced the idea that Chinese phones have a significant lead when it comes to the cameras.

Connectivity is a mixed bag (yet again)

You don't need me to tell you about the state of the cellular modem on Pixels. With Google switching to a MediaTek modem this year, I thought the Pixel 11 Pro XL would be on par with other high-end phones. While connectivity is better, it wasn't as reliable as other devices I used in recent months.

I routinely saw an LTE signal in areas where I used to get 5G, and even at home, the signal was spotty. The phone intermittently disconnected from my home network, and I had to manually toggle the internet tile to get it to register on the network again. I get that these are minor quibbles, but I don't want to see any of these issues on a $1,199 phone — no other flagship has these problems.

Battery life is better than I imagined

The 5,115mAh battery on the Pixel 11 Pro XL is relatively smaller (the Find X9 Ultra has a 7,000mAh unit), but thanks to efficiency gains this year, it manages to last an entire day (and a bit) without any problems.

I got a full day of use even while traveling, and charging it wasn't as much of a hassle — it takes just an hour to fully charge the battery. On busy days that involve taking hundreds of photos, the Pixel 11 Pro XL managed to last until the night.

Qi 2.2 integration is a big deal, and not having to use a case makes a real difference. I use Qi 2.2 power banks and chargers daily, and as someone who doesn't like using cases, it's great to see native integration on the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

The software continues to be the real highlight

The main reason I use Pixels is the software, and there's a lot to like in Android 17. Most of the new features are around AI (which I don't need or use), but Rambler in Gboard is incredibly good, and I need it on other Android devices and the iPhone. I like that Google doesn't have any bloatware, and the interface itself is clean, has bright colors, and is highly customizable.

Using the Pixel 11 Pro XL made me realize that Google really needs to launch a Pixel Ultra to take on its Chinese rivals. While the phone does a good job against the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the Galaxy S26 Ultra, it doesn't have an answer to the Find X9 Ultra, Vivo X300 Ultra, and the Xiaomi 17 Ultra, and Google needs to rectify that in coming years.

Although the brand always focused on software to make up the difference with cameras, we are getting to the point with diminishing returns, and Google needs to start using higher-resolution modules and generally deliver better camera hardware.

Google
Pixel 11 Pro XL

The Pixel 11 Pro XL is a great choice if you're on an older device and are considering an upgrade. It may not be as good as its Chinese rivals, but it is much better than its predecessors.

item.title: I have no idea how Meta made a VR headset that's 83% lighter and 60% smaller than Apple Vision Pro, but I'm all here for it
item.dc:content:
The era of giant, heavy VR headsets is officially over. The Oculus Quest began the era of standalone VR headsets in 2019, and now Meta VR Glasses will begin the era of tiny, comfortable standalone headsets when they launch in Spring 2027.

Despite what the name implies, Meta VR Glasses aren't associated with the company's other wearables offerings from brands like Ray-Ban and Oakley. Operationally, these are essentially a Meta Quest headset without the Quest branding, clearly separating it from that product line and giving it a new identity.

While Quest became most popular with kids and teenagers, Meta is aiming its new VR Glasses squarely at adults who want a cutting-edge immersive experience. It has brand-new features, content partnerships with streaming companies and sports leagues, and 75 new hand-tracking games at launch (including new Ace Attorney VR and Two Point Hospital VR, to name two).

All that, plus 100% backward compatibility with existing Meta Quest apps and games. It's a monumental moment for VR and the culmination of everything Meta has built up to this point.

The lightest standalone VR headset ever

When Apple Vision Pro launched, it blew people away. The experience was revolutionary, but its 600g weight and $3500 price tag severely diminished its appeal. Samsung's Galaxy XR launched last year at half the price, but it still weighed 545g and doesn't have the gaming support of Meta's platform.

Meta VR Glasses weigh just 100g. They're also less than half the size of either Apple's or Samsung's headsets. They also come in two sizes to accommodate as many people as possible and don't need an uncomfortable head strap to keep the VR Glasses on your face.

Instead, Meta VR Glasses look and feel more like a pair of glasses than a headset. Each temple arm folds in like a pair of glasses, and they even use adjustable nose pads. They're not intended to be worn all day like Meta AI Glasses, though. These are still VR headsets, just without all the bulk and weight the category has become synonymous with.

Prescription lenses magnetically attach to the headset's lenses, making fitting and sharing a breeze. The 5K micro-OLED panels inside each lens are incredibly bright and crisp, sporting a 37 pixels-per-degree (PPD) resolution. By comparison, Quest 3 has just 20 PPD, while Apple Vision Pro has around 34 PPD.

The trick here is that Meta reduced the FoV to achieve this level of clarity. At 85 degrees, it's around 11 degrees narrower than Quest 3S and 25 degrees narrower than Quest 3. It felt narrower than Quest, for sure, but not as narrow as even the best smart glasses. You adjust the IPD by manually sliding the lenses.

Meta VR Glasses don't ship with controllers, but you can pair them with any existing Quest 3-era controller or order a separate pair. I got to play a new version of Beat Saber called Beat Saber Flux, which is hand-tracking-only and heavily modifies the gameplay to match hand tracking's vibe. If you're familiar with Synth Riders, this new Beat Saber will feel familiar.

I also got to see an upcoming mixed reality title called Dice Throne Digital, a video game version of the popular Dice Throne board game. This roguelike title is like "battle Yatzi," as the developers described it to me: you grab imaginary dice, shake them violently in your hand, and throw them anywhere in your room.

Thanks to Meta's continuously improved hand tracking — plus the power of the new Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset inside Meta VR Glasses — the action looks more visceral than I ever thought a hand-tracking game could. Watch your hand transform into a powerful glowing fist when you shake the dice, and watch them bounce off your real-world objects as if they actually existed.

The new chipset and battery are housed in a separate, phone-sized compute puck that clips onto a belt or pocket. Ventilation on top of the puck keeps things cool, and a USB-C port on the bottom can power the headset indefinitely with a 45W charger. It even supports USB-C video input, so you can plug in your Steam Deck and get a massive 5K resolution screen anywhere.

Meta intends this headset to be used primarily while seated, so you'll likely want a "proper" headset for fully immersive VR experiences (read: ones you physically walk around, duck, or look under objects). Magnetic light blockers (like on Meta Quest Pro) will make things even more immersive, but I didn't get to see either of these at my hands-on.

The UI is the same as on existing Quest headsets, but built-in eye tracking capabilities and new cameras make navigating truly effortless. No need to raise your hand anymore; just look at what you want to select and pinch your thumb and index finger together, or make a fist and use your thumb like a D-pad to scroll. Meta VR Glasses will even create a virtual mouse and keyboard on any surface, both of which worked unbelievably well in my demo.

Speaking of cinema-grade experiences, Meta is clearly aiming this headset at a more casual crowd than the folks who normally enjoy the highly active gaming experiences synonymous with VR. Meta VR Glasses are designed primarily as a private screen, delivering IMAX-quality visuals with native 12-bit micro-OLED panels, all of which are James Cameron-certified (seriously!).

The displays use a PWM dimming method that matches the refresh rate, which lines up with how its LCD-based headsets have always worked. This should be comfortable for most people, including PWM-sensitive people like me. That's great since the 3-hour battery life and more casual use cases will likely have you in the headset for hours at a time.

A key part of this experience is a bespoke selection of included services, such as courtside seats at NBA games included in the headset's price (no additional subscription required). I don't know how many games this service will cover, but the game I watched in the headset felt like I was right next to the celebrities who can afford front-row tickets.

Meta VR Glasses are a total reboot of the VR paradigm Meta has been selling, and the company is putting high hopes in this product being a smash hit. The $1,299 price will limit its appeal a bit, but this is the most cutting-edge VR headset I've used in my 11 years covering VR professionally, and it finally solves the weight and size problem people have been asking for.
item.description: Meta VR Glasses are the newest VR headsets from Meta, and they're like nothing you've ever seen before.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Sutrich
item.dc:description: <p>Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Because of this, he covers both smartphones and VR technology, two avenues that split his passions right down the middle. From Nokia fan to Android fanatic, Nick has been writing about and reviewing smartphones since 2011. An avid gamer and equally well-versed tech head, Nick worked in the IT industry for 15 years, helping to further develop his technical knowledge, which has become particularly important in his fight with PWM sensitivity and deep dives into display technology. He's a huge fan of any phone that can fold in half and loves getting into the nitty-gritty with folding phone coverage for the site. He's also got over a decade of experience with VR gaming, having used the original Oculus DK1 and every major VR headset since then, passionately covering Android Central's Meta Quest content and smart glasses coverage with his weekly thVRsday column on Thursdays. Beyond that, you'll find Nick taking photos of anything and everything, from the beautiful mountains of his home to the chickens in his backyard, and using them to compare cameras to help you choose the best one.</p>
